options.explanation: Each copper carries +1 to balance the oxide's -2.
That name belongs to CuO, the black oxide.

options.explanation: The metal is the positive partner.
The sulfate ion's -2 forces manganese to +2.
That is the manganate(VII) value, not the sulfate.
No such state appears in this salt.

questions.stem: Why does KMnO4 earn the name potassium manganate(VII)?

options.explanation: The Roman numeral reports the state in this compound only.
The numeral reports an oxidation number, not a count.

options.text: Potassium's +1 leaves MnO4- at -1, forcing Mn to +7
options.explanation: The ion arithmetic lands on seven.
Each oxygen gives -2.

questions.stem: When sodium reacts with water, what happens to sodium's oxidation number?

options.explanation: Metals never go negative here.
Sodium ends as Na+ in NaOH.
Sodium only ever shows +1.

options.text: It rises from 0 to +1 as sodium loses an electron
options.explanation: Electron loss is the cation-forming oxidation.

questions.stem: Which change marks a non-metal forming an anion?

options.text: Its oxidation number decreases as it gains electrons
options.explanation: Electron gain reduces the species.

options.text: Its oxidation number increases as it loses electrons
options.explanation: That describes metal cation formation.
The anion carries a charge.
Anion formation produces a charged species.

questions.stem: Name MnSO4 and Na2Cr2O7 using Stock notation.
questions.modelAnswer: MnSO4 is manganese(II) sulfate and Na2Cr2O7 is sodium dichromate(VI).

questions.stem: State what happens to oxidation numbers when metals form cations and non-metals form anions.
questions.modelAnswer: Metals are oxidised as their number increases; non-metals are reduced as their number decreases.

questions.stem: Explain why the oxidation number of a metal rises when it forms an ion.
questions.modelAnswer: Losing electrons strips negative charge from the neutral atom, so its notional ionic charge rises by one unit per electron surrendered.

questions.stem: In Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2, magnesium climbs 0 to +2. How many electrons does one magnesium atom surrender, and to which species?
questions.modelAnswer: One magnesium atom surrenders 2 electrons, accepted by the hydrogen ions that become H2.

questions.stem: What does a half equation show?

options.text: Two species exchanging electrons at once
options.explanation: Both legs in one line is not a half.

options.text: Only one half of an electron transfer, one species gaining or losing electrons
options.explanation: Each half isolates one leg of the transfer.
That is the full equation's job.
Charges and electrons are the half's essence.

questions.stem: Which sequence lists the four steps for a complicated half equation?

options.explanation: The key atom is balanced first.
Half equations in acid use H+, not OH-.

options.text: Balance the key atom, add H2O for oxygen, add H+ for hydrogen, add e- for charge
options.explanation: The order is atom, water, hydrogen ion, electron.

options.text: Add e- first, then H2O, then H+
options.explanation: Electrons come last, after charge is known.

questions.stem: In the dichromate half, why do 14 H+ ions appear?

options.explanation: The electrons number 6, not 14.
The ion holds only 7 oxygens.
Hydrogen balance fixes it exactly.

options.text: Seven waters hold 14 hydrogens, so 14 H+ balance the right side's hydrogens
options.explanation: Each water carries 2 hydrogens.

options.text: The dichromate half carries 6 electrons, so six 1-electron oxidations must match it
options.explanation: Equal electron counts are the cancellation condition.

Charge balance comes from the H+ and e- terms.

options.text: Six is the convention for all iron reactions
options.explanation: Scaling follows the ledger, not convention.

questions.stem: What must be true of the electrons in the two combined halves?

options.explanation: Electrons never convert into molecules.

options.text: Their counts are equal, so they cancel and vanish from the sum

questions.stem: Write the two half equations for the dichromate-iron(II) reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Fe2+ -> Fe3+ + e- and Cr2O7 2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O are the two halves.

questions.stem: State what an ionic equation shows that a full equation does not.
questions.modelAnswer: An ionic equation prints the reacting ions alone, with every spectator species stripped away.

questions.stem: Explain why water and hydrogen ions appear in some half equations but not others.
questions.modelAnswer: Simple ion-electron transfers balance directly, but oxygen-bearing ions carry O atoms that no bare electron can balance, so water absorbs the oxygen and H+ absorbs the hydrogen the water introduced.

questions.stem: The dichromate half accepts 6 electrons. If a permanganate half accepts 5, how many iron(II) oxidations must it partner?
questions.modelAnswer: Five 1-electron oxidations match the 5-electron reduction, so five Fe2+ ions partner one MnO4-.

questions.stem: How many units does manganese fall in the manganate-iron reaction?

options.explanation: No elemental manganese forms.
No MnO2 appears in acid solution here.
The fall fixes the ledger's down-leg.

questions.stem: Why does the ledger force five iron(II) climbs per manganate fall?

options.explanation: Mass never sets stoichiometry.
It holds four, and oxygen does not set the ratio.
The ratio comes from the arithmetic, not convention.

options.text: Iron climbs 1 unit per atom, so five atoms supply the 5 units manganese releases
options.explanation: The ledger equalises at five climbs per fall.

questions.stem: How many H+ ions does the balanced equation carry on the left?

options.explanation: Charge balance plus the water census land on eight.

options.explanation: Acidic half equations use water, not hydroxide.
Four waters absorb the ion's four oxygens and eight hydrogens.

options.explanation: Charge census must also close.
Appearance is not verification.

options.text: Charge -1 + 10 + 8 = +17 matches +2 + 15 = +17, and atoms close 1 Mn, 5 Fe, 4 O, 8 H

questions.stem: Write the balanced ionic equation for MnO4- reacting with Fe2+ in acid.
questions.modelAnswer: MnO4- + 5Fe2+ + 8H+ -> Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O is the balanced ionic equation.

questions.stem: State the oxidation-number changes that drive the 1:5 ratio.
questions.modelAnswer: Manganese falls from +7 to +2, a 5-unit drop, while each iron rises from +2 to +3, a 1-unit climb.

questions.stem: Explain why the direct method needs no explicit half equations.
questions.modelAnswer: The oxidation-number ledger already contains everything the halves would say: the unit changes and their ratio - so scaling and charge patching can proceed straight to the balanced equation.

questions.stem: If a different oxidising agent fell only 3 units per ion, how many Fe2+ would each such ion oxidise?
questions.modelAnswer: Three 1-unit climbs per 3-unit fall give three Fe2+ per oxidising ion.
